items.stem: A compliance team requires that every AI-flagged transaction above a risk threshold pass through a two-person sequential review, the second reviewer blind to the first, under a documented regulatory audit expectation. How should the architect handle this review workflow?

opts.t: Continue eliciting the cost of a missed versus falsely flagged transaction, since that determines the review workflow design.
Implement the two-person sequential blind review exactly as specified; it is the compliance-driven requirement, not an implementation suggestion to optimize.
Propose a confidence-weighted single-reviewer model that the architect judges more efficient, then present it as an improvement to the sponsor.
Escalate to the sponsor's leadership that the two-step sequential requirement is unnecessarily slow and should be reconsidered before build starts.

items.whyRight: The two-person sequential blind review is tied to a documented regulatory audit expectation, so it is the actual requirement, not the sponsor's guess at how to satisfy some looser goal. A more elegant single-reviewer redesign is out of scope, however sound the engineering.

whyWrong.A: This treats an already-specified, regulator-tied workflow as still unbounded, when the mechanism itself, not its cost basis, is the fixed requirement here.
whyWrong.C: Replacing the mandated workflow with a more efficient design substitutes the architect's preference for a compliance-driven mechanism the sponsor cannot trade away.
whyWrong.D: Framing a regulatory audit expectation as a build-schedule inconvenience to negotiate away misreads it as a preference rather than a fixed constraint.

items.t1Clause: under a documented regulatory audit expectation
items.factAnswerRaw: Implement the two-person sequential blind review exactly as specified; it is the compliance-driven requirement, not an implementation suggestion to optimize.

items.stem: A sponsor's risk committee has mandated that this system's monthly governance report show the end-to-end error rate after human review, computed against the full production population, per the committee's charter. How should the architect handle this month's report?

opts.t: Report accuracy broken out by document type with the end-to-end outcome, since segmentation is generally the more informative reporting practice.
Decline to finalize this month's report until the committee agrees to add per-segment breakdowns alongside the mandated figure.
Produce the end-to-end error rate after human review exactly as specified; the mandated metric and cadence are the governance requirement.
Propose adding a composite risk score the architect judges more informative, alongside the committee's requested figure.

items.whyRight: The committee's charter names the exact metric and cadence, so that mechanism is the governance requirement itself, not the sponsor's rough idea of what a report should contain. A more segmented or additional metric, however useful, is out of scope for this deliverable.

whyWrong.A: Segmentation is the right move only when no specific metric has been mandated; here it substitutes the architect's own report design for a chartered requirement.
whyWrong.B: Withholding the mandated report over a preferred addition treats a governance requirement as negotiable, delaying a deliverable the committee is entitled to on schedule.
whyWrong.D: Adding a metric nobody chartered is a more elaborate report than requested, not a compliant one; the committee asked for one specific figure.

items.factAnswerRaw: Produce the end-to-end error rate after human review exactly as specified; the mandated metric and cadence are the governance requirement.

items.stem: A recurring review tracks the system's satisfaction metric for a rollout decision. The sponsor cites last month's uptick as proof the triage-flow change fixed the issue, but that month saw a seasonal drop in case volume skewed toward routine cases. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Accept the uptick as evidence the triage-flow change fixed the issue and report the improvement to the sponsor's steering group.
Compare the metric against the same low-volume period in prior cycles before attributing the uptick to the triage-flow change.
Establish a new recurring review that reports real production performance against the agreed criteria.
Tell the sponsor that satisfaction upticks cannot be attributed to any process change without a controlled experiment.

items.whyRight: The recurring review's metric is correctly defined and tracking the real signal; the error is attributing a single period's uptick to the change without ruling out the seasonal volume dip that shifted the case mix toward easier work.

whyWrong.A: The stem's own evidence, a seasonal volume dip skewing the case mix toward routine work, already undercuts crediting the change; the uptick has an unruled-out alternative cause.
whyWrong.C: A recurring review already exists here; the gap is not a missing loop but crediting a single reading of it to the wrong cause.
whyWrong.D: The existing recurring measurement can settle this without a new experiment; refusing to read the metric at all abandons the analysis the sponsor needs.

items.t1Clause: that month saw a seasonal drop in case volume skewed toward routine cases
items.factAnswerRaw: Compare the metric against the same low-volume period in prior cycles before attributing the uptick to the triage-flow change.

items.stem: A latency ceiling that drove a model-tier choice a year ago has been relaxed. The only design record is a recorded walkthrough; the component diagrams are unchanged. What should the architect have recorded to make this decision reopenable?

opts.t: Record the decision, the rejected alternatives with their numbers, the trade-off accepted, and the latency ceiling that drove the choice.
Check the recorded constraint and re-evaluate the decision now that the ceiling has changed.
Produce a comprehensive written description of the current architecture with detailed component diagrams for the receiving team.
Hold another recorded walkthrough covering the new latency ceiling and how it affects the design.

items.whyRight: A decision record needs the decision, the rejected alternatives with their numbers, the trade-off accepted, and the constraint that drove the choice; only that lets the team check the ceiling change against the original reasoning and reopen the decision on evidence.

whyWrong.B: No constraint was ever recorded here, only a walkthrough was held, so there is nothing written to check against the new latency ceiling.
whyWrong.C: A thorough description of the current design, however detailed, carries no reasoning; it cannot show whether the relaxed ceiling changes the original trade-off.
whyWrong.D: A second walkthrough transfers understanding once more to whoever attends, but leaves no written record the next reviewer can check against a future change.

items.t1Clause: the only design record is a recorded walkthrough

items.stem: A 60-user pilot succeeds and is approved for rollout to 900 users. During the pilot, a 1-in-400 failure recurred twice in 150 cases, and human review absorbed 18% of pilot volume. Select two actions to take before rollout.

opts.t: Treat the observed failure rate and review proportion as fixed percentages that hold unchanged at higher volume.
Plan for the 1-in-400 failure as a routine event at the new volume, not as a rare edge case.
Convert the 18% review proportion observed in the pilot into a staffing line sized to the projected rollout volume.
Size infrastructure capacity and rate limits for the new volume, and treat that as the binding constraint on readiness.

items.whyRight: A failure recurring twice in a 150-case pilot is frequent at fifteen times the volume, so it must be planned as routine, not rare. The review load actually measured in the pilot is the only sound basis for staffing the wider rollout.

whyWrong.A: The observed rates are exactly what must be re-examined at the new scale, not treated as fixed; freezing them skips the assumption audit that scaling requires.
whyWrong.D: Infrastructure and rate-limit sizing is real and necessary, but it is not the binding constraint here; the failure rate and review load are what actually bite at this scale.

items.t1Clause: human review absorbed 18% of pilot volume
items.factAnswerRaw: Plan for it as a routine event; Convert to a staffing line at projected volume before rollout
